title: Stacking & Blending
tagline: Train a model whose only job is to learn how to best combine your other models.
what_it_is: Stacking (and its simpler cousin, blending) is an ensemble technique where predictions from several different base models are used as input features to train a final 'meta-model,' which learns the best way to combine them into one final prediction.
key_points: Different from bagging/boosting — stacking combines outputs of different types of models, not many copies of the same one.
Base models (e.g. Random Forest, SVM, logistic regression) each make predictions; those predictions become inputs to the meta-model.
The meta-model learns which base models to trust more in which situations, rather than a simple average or vote.
Blending is a simpler variant that uses a held-out validation set instead of full cross-validation to generate meta-features.
Adds complexity and inference cost — used mainly when squeezing out the last bit of accuracy matters.
why_it_exists: Different model types make different kinds of mistakes — a tree-based model and a linear model fail on different examples. Stacking exists to let a learned meta-model exploit those different failure patterns, rather than combining models with a fixed rule like simple averaging or majority voting.
intuition: Imagine a panel of three expert consultants, each with a different specialty, giving their opinion on a business decision. Instead of just averaging their opinions equally, you hire a fourth expert whose entire job is to learn, over time, which consultant to trust more in which situations — that fourth expert is the meta-model.

steps.title: Train base models
steps.description: Train several different models (e.g. Random Forest, SVM, k-NN) on the training data using cross-validation to avoid leakage.

steps.title: Generate meta-features
steps.description: Use each base model's out-of-fold predictions as new input features for the meta-model.

steps.title: Train the meta-model
steps.description: Fit a typically simple model (e.g. logistic regression) on these meta-features to produce the final prediction.

steps.title: Predict on new data
steps.description: At inference time, run new data through all base models first, then feed their outputs into the trained meta-model.

when_to_use: Use in competitions or high-stakes production systems where the last percent of accuracy justifies the added complexity.
Use when your base models make genuinely different kinds of errors — stacking gains little if they all fail on the same examples.
when_not_to_use: Do not use stacking when model interpretability or simplicity matters — it's one of the least explainable approaches.
Do not use it without proper cross-validation to generate meta-features — using in-sample predictions leaks information and overstates performance.
Do not use it in latency-sensitive systems without accounting for the added inference cost of running multiple models.
common_mistakes: Generating meta-features using the base models' training-set predictions directly, leaking information and inflating meta-model performance.
Stacking many highly correlated base models that all make the same mistakes — gains little over a single model.
Overcomplicating a pipeline with stacking when a single well-tuned gradient boosting model would perform nearly as well.
ds_usage: A common technique in Kaggle-style machine learning competitions and select high-value production systems, though rarely used in early-stage or resource-constrained projects due to its added complexity.
